questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) What does deadlock mean in process management? (1 marks)

(b) Draw a resources allocation diagram with three processes ($P_1$, $P_2$ and $P_3$) and three resources ($R_1$, $R_2$ and $R_3$), each having one instance, where the three processes are deadlocked. In your diagram, $P_1$ should be holding the resources $R_2$ and requesting for $R_1$. (3 marks)

(c) How could an operating system recover from a deadlock situation? (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Deadlock (1 mark)**

A deadlock is a situation in which two or more processes are blocked **for ever**, because each of them is holding a resource and waiting for a resource that is held by another process of the group, so none of them can continue.

**(b) Resource allocation diagram (3 marks)**

Notation: a circle is a process, a rectangle is a resource (with one instance, one dot); an arrow from a process to a resource is a **request** edge; an arrow from a resource to a process is an **assignment** edge (the process holds the resource).

```text
                   request                  assignment
        (P1) ------------------> [R1] ------------------> (P2)
         ^                                                  |
         | assignment                               request |
         |                                                  v
        [R2] <------------------ (P3) <------------------ [R3]
                   request                  assignment
```

The edges are:

- $R_2 \to P_1$ ($P_1$ holds $R_2$) and $P_1 \to R_1$ ($P_1$ requests $R_1$);
- $R_1 \to P_2$ ($P_2$ holds $R_1$) and $P_2 \to R_3$ ($P_2$ requests $R_3$);
- $R_3 \to P_3$ ($P_3$ holds $R_3$) and $P_3 \to R_2$ ($P_3$ requests $R_2$).

The graph contains the cycle $P_1 \to R_1 \to P_2 \to R_3 \to P_3 \to R_2 \to P_1$. Since every resource has only one instance, this cycle means that the three processes are deadlocked: $P_1$ waits for $P_2$, $P_2$ waits for $P_3$ and $P_3$ waits for $P_1$ (the four conditions of deadlock are met: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no pre-emption, circular wait).

**(c) Recovery from deadlock (3 marks)**

- **Process termination:** the operating system aborts all the deadlocked processes, or, more economically, aborts one process at a time (chosen by priority, time already used, number of resources held) until the cycle is broken; the resources of the aborted process are released.
- **Resource pre-emption:** a resource is taken from one deadlocked process and given to another so that it can finish; the first process is rolled back to a safe state (checkpoint) and restarted later. The OS must avoid always choosing the same victim (starvation).
- **Rollback / restart:** the system is restored to a previous checkpoint, or in the last resort the system is rebooted or the operator intervenes manually.

Any three well explained methods score the 3 marks.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Jobs $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ need 6, 4 and 3 units of execution time respectively. They arrive at time units 1, 4 and 7.

(a) Which job is completed last if each executes for at most 2 time units at a time? (2 marks)

(b) Draw a Gantt chart for job execution if a Round Robin scheduling algorithm is used with a time quantum of 2 time units. (4 marks)

(c) Calculate the average turnaround time for each of the processes. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Simulation of Round Robin (quantum = 2).** Convention used: a process that arrives at the same instant as a pre-empted process is placed in the ready queue **before** it. The processor is idle until time 1.

| Time | Event | Ready queue after the event |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $P_1$ arrives and runs (1 to 3), 4 units left | $P_1$ |
| 3 | $P_1$ is alone, so it runs again (3 to 5), 2 units left; $P_2$ arrives at 4 | $P_2$, $P_1$ |
| 5 | $P_2$ runs (5 to 7), 2 units left; $P_3$ arrives at 7 | $P_1$, $P_3$, $P_2$ |
| 7 | $P_1$ runs (7 to 9) and **finishes at 9** | $P_3$, $P_2$ |
| 9 | $P_3$ runs (9 to 11), 1 unit left | $P_2$, $P_3$ |
| 11 | $P_2$ runs (11 to 13) and **finishes at 13** | $P_3$ |
| 13 | $P_3$ runs (13 to 14) and **finishes at 14** | empty |

**(a) Job completed last (2 marks)**

The completion times are $P_1$ = 9, $P_2$ = 13 and $P_3$ = 14. The job completed last is **$P_3$**, at time 14 (it is also the last job to arrive and it still needs one more slice after the others).

**(b) Gantt chart (4 marks)**

```text
| idle | P1 | P1 | P2 | P1 | P3 | P2 | P3 |
0      1    3    5    7    9    11   13   14
```

| Time interval | 0-1 | 1-3 | 3-5 | 5-7 | 7-9 | 9-11 | 11-13 | 13-14 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Process running | idle | $P_1$ | $P_1$ | $P_2$ | $P_1$ | $P_3$ | $P_2$ | $P_3$ |

($P_1$ is executed twice in a row, 1 to 3 and 3 to 5, because no other process is ready at time 3.)

**(c) Turnaround times (4 marks)**

Turnaround time = completion time - arrival time.

| Process | Arrival | Completion | Turnaround |
|---|---|---|---|
| $P_1$ | 1 | 9 | $9 - 1 = 8$ |
| $P_2$ | 4 | 13 | $13 - 4 = 9$ |
| $P_3$ | 7 | 14 | $14 - 7 = 7$ |

$$\text{Average turnaround time} = \frac{8 + 9 + 7}{3} = \frac{24}{3} = 8 \text{ time units}$$

(Remark: if a process that arrives at the same instant as a pre-empted process were queued *after* it, $P_2$ would finish at 11, with turnaround time 7, and the average would be $22/3 \approx 7.33$; the order of completion and the last job, $P_3$, do not change.)
